data.title: After Intel's historic stock drop, analysts say there's no reason to buy the dip
data.description:
By Britney Nguyen

'A cheaper stock does not necessarily offer better value,' one expert says

Intel, led by CEO Lip-Bu Tan, disappointed investors with its latest forecast.

Even in the wake of what could be Intel's worst daily stock drop in decades, some analysts say investors should steer clear.

"A cheaper stock does not necessarily offer better value," Dan Kemp, founder of investment consultancy Portfolio Thinking, told MarketWatch.

Intel's (INTC) earnings report on Thursday afternoon shed light on various problems, including a dramatically weakening market for personal-computer chips and a server business that's leaving money on the table because it can't meet all its demand. Intel is also losing money on an expensive chip-manufacturing business that remains a work in progress.

Seaport Research analyst Jay Goldberg thinks that Intel "will sort itself out" eventually, but its comeback "is taking too long."

The company's current challenges, which partly stem from poor foresight into market conditions that has left the company without enough manufacturing capacity for its critical AI server chips, have put a dent in the turnaround efforts undertaken by CEO Lip-Bu Tan.

Goldberg, who just lowered his rating on Intel to neutral from buy, said he sees "no reason to own the stock" as the company works through its issues.

Intel's 29% stock drop as of midday Friday puts it on pace for its worst one-day decline since at least 1980, according to Dow Jones Market Data. It also draws flashbacks to August 2024, when Intel shares shed 26% in a single day upon suspending its dividend and beginning a massive cost-cutting program.

To the company's credit, Intel is in better shape than it was two years ago, Goldberg said. Its chip-manufacturing technology is gaining traction with customers and producing better yields, he said, referring to the amount of usable chips that come from a single wafer. The commentary around its chip-manufacturing business "gives us further confidence that Intel Foundry will be viable, some day," Goldberg said in a note to clients.

That prospect alone may not be reason to buy into Intel's stock now, however.

Intel on Thursday said that persistent weakness in demand for PCs, spurred by rising memory prices, was partly to blame for a forecast that came short of what analysts had been expecting.

There are also constraints throughout its supply chain, the company noted, including for chip wafers and packaging substrates - an essential component for its advanced chip packaging technology that is gaining appeal with customers.

Intel had indicated the previous quarter it was getting back on track with supply, Goldberg said - but the third-quarter results showed that hasn't happened.

While Intel has upped production of client wafers for the PC market, which "is seeing its worst downturn" in more than a decade, it is facing shortages of wafers for data-center server central processing units to support an artificial-intelligence market that "is seeing its greatest cycle ever," he noted.

"Where they really lost us was management's commentary that supply would not come into balance until the middle of next year," he said, also noting that Intel said its investments in long-term assets to benefit the business could weigh on its cash flow, or the money it generates after that spending and operating expenses.

Although the stock's steep drop on Friday follows its less-than-stellar report, it also has to do with investors realizing "the size of the mountain Intel must climb over the next decade to justify its previous valuation," Portfolio Thinking's Kemp said.

At Intel's current valuation, the market needs Intel Foundry to bring in $14 billion a year, Kemp said - a high mark for a business that has lost money for several consecutive quarters and generated external revenue of just $411 million in the September quarter.

While the selloff could look like a bargain to some investors, Kemp said its important to distinguish between that and a discount.

Indeed, Intel shares now trade at 35.9x estimated forward earnings, down from 43.8x heading into the report on Thursday, according to Dow Jones Market Data. But the earnings also made investors call into question trends like its ability to capitalize appropriately on a wave of demand for server CPUs, something that had previously helped drive its valuation higher.

Richard Windsor, founder of research firm Radio Free Mobile, shared similar caution about the stock given his view that while Tan has made progress on a turnaround, "he is not out of the woods yet."

The stock's high valuation, Intel's weak projections for next year and the ongoing debate over the dominance of its x86 chip architecture "leaves me cautious on the shares," Windsor said in a note to clients.

Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya also lowered his rating on Intel's stock to neutral from a previous buy position.

Intel's PC weakness "more than" offsets the strength it is showing in its data-center and AI segment, Arya said in a note to clients.

And even as it benefits from AI-driven demand for server CPUs, Intel faces component-supply issues there, while its offerings "are not yet technically competitive" with those from CPU rivals Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Arm (ARM), according to Arya.

-Britney Nguyen

This content was created by MarketWatch, which is operated by Dow Jones & Co. MarketWatch is published independently from Dow Jones Newswires and The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: United States Lime & Minerals Reports Q3 Revenue Growth and Lower Net Income
data.description:
United States Lime & Minerals reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $106.2 million, up 4.1% year over year, while net income declined 1.9% to $38.0 million. Diluted earnings per share were $1.32, compared with $1.35 a year earlier. The company also declared a regular quarterly cash dividend.

Financial Highlights

  • Third-quarter revenue rose 4.1% to $106.2 million; revenue for the first nine months increased 2.9% to $293.1 million.
  • Third-quarter gross profit was $50.8 million, compared with $52.2 million a year earlier. Nine-month gross profit was $139.2 million, versus $140.2 million.
  • Operating profit was $44.7 million for the quarter and $121.1 million for the first nine months, compared with $46.3 million and $121.8 million, respectively, in 2025.
  • Third-quarter net income was $38.0 million, or $1.32 per diluted share; nine-month net income was $103.1 million, or $3.58 per diluted share.
  • The board declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.06 per share, payable December 11, 2026, to shareholders of record November 20, 2026.

Business Highlights

  • Quarterly sales volumes and average selling prices increased modestly. Stronger steel-customer demand supported volumes, partially offset by weaker demand from construction customers.
  • For the first nine months, higher steel-customer demand was partly offset by reduced demand from roof shingle customers.
  • The new kiln at the Texas facility began intermittently producing quicklime during the quarter. Final commissioning is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter.
  • Integrating the new kiln into existing Texas operations caused production inefficiencies. Higher transportation and fuel costs, particularly diesel, also affected operations.
  • Management cited delays to some large construction projects, including permitting, and is monitoring signs of slowing residential construction in Texas.

Original SEC Filing: UNITED STATES LIME & MINERALS INC [ USLM ] - 8-K - Oct. 30, 2026

data.title: Peoples Financial Services Reports Q3 Net Income of $19.1 Million
data.description:
Peoples Financial Services reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $19.1 million, or $1.90 per diluted share, up from $15.2 million, or $1.51 per diluted share, a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, net income was $48.7 million, or $4.85 per diluted share. Growth in net interest and noninterest income contributed to the results.

Financial Highlights

  • Third-quarter net interest income was $47.3 million, compared with $41.2 million in the year-ago quarter; nine-month net interest income was $135.8 million, up from $122.9 million.
  • Net income for the quarter rose 25.5% to $19.1 million. Nine-month net income increased 3.1% to $48.7 million.
  • Diluted earnings per share were $1.90 for the quarter and $4.85 for the first nine months. Core diluted earnings per share, a non-GAAP measure, were $1.90 and $4.81, respectively.
  • Third-quarter net interest margin on a fully taxable equivalent basis was 3.80%, up from 3.54% a year earlier. The nine-month margin was 3.77%, compared with 3.58%.
  • Noninterest income was $5.7 million for the quarter and $19.1 million for the first nine months. Noninterest expense was $31.7 million and $92.2 million, respectively.

Business Highlights

  • Total loans grew compared with both the prior quarter and prior-year quarter, with growth across commercial and residential real estate, commercial and industrial, and municipal lending.
  • Deposits increased from the prior quarter and year-ago period. The company reported a strategic deposit-growth effort and a lower share of brokered deposits than in the prior quarter.
  • Asset quality improved: nonperforming assets declined from both June 2026 and September 2025, reflecting resolutions of nonaccrual assets and a foreclosed property.
  • The company recorded a third-quarter benefit for credit losses, citing improved asset-quality measures, seasoning in the equipment-loan segment, and lower specific reserves following resolutions of nonperforming loans.
  • Peoples continued investing in operations, including an online account-opening platform; it also cited higher data-processing costs associated with the platform’s implementation.

data.title: AI spending fears spark tech selloff, defensives shine
data.description:
Key points:
  • Main US indexes decline; Nasdaq off most, ending down ~2.9%
  • Tech is weakest S&P 500 sector; energy is the leading gainer
  • Dollar gains; US crude rises; bitcoin falls ~2.5%; gold drops ~3.5%
  • US 10-year Treasury yield falls to ~4.93%

AI SPENDING FEARS SPARK TECH SELLOFF, DEFENSIVES SHINE

US stocks tumbled Friday, with the Nasdaq falling to a three-month low after disappointing results from Intel and Amazon intensified concerns about the enormous sums being poured into AI and when, or whether, those investments will begin to pay off.

The damage was concentrated in technology, but it was severe. Both the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 CBOE:SPX suffered their biggest daily declines since early June. The technology sector fell more than 4%, marking its worst one-day drop since then.

Despite the tech selloff, much of the broader market held up relatively well. A majority of S&P 500 sectors finished in positive territory, led by energy and consumer staples , both of which gained more than 1%.

Chip stocks bore the brunt of the selling. The PHLX Semiconductor Index plunged more than 7% for its biggest daily percentage drop since late June. Precious metals miners were also caught up in the selloff, with the PHLX Gold/Silver Miners Index (.XAU) tumbling more than 5%.

There were still a few bright spots. Housing-related shares and transports managed to end the session modestly higher, while the S&P 500's energy and healthcare sectors closed at fresh record highs. The Dividend Aristocrats ETF also notched a record close.

In many ways, October lived up to its reputation for volatility and a preference for defense. The Dividend Aristocrats ETF posted its biggest monthly gain since October 2022, while the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF enjoyed its strongest month since December 2021. At the same time, the iShares Momentum Factor ETF slumped more than 10%, highlighting just how sharply leadership shifted during the month.

For the week, all three major indexes finished lower.

October was especially tough on growth-oriented stocks. The Nasdaq posted its biggest monthly decline since March 2025, while the S&P 500 also ended the month lower. The Dow , however, managed to finish October in positive territory.

Meanwhile, Treasury yields reflected a similar move toward safety. The 10-year Treasury yield is down nearly 37 basis points for the month, on track for its biggest monthly decline since December 2023.

data.title: Wall Street closes sharply lower as AI cash burn fears spark tech selloff
data.description:
Key points:
  • Indexes down: Dow 1.09%, S&P 500 1.82%, Nasdaq 2.86%
  • Nasdaq posts largest one-day percentage drop since early June
  • Intel slides after reporting big cash burn
  • Crypto firms slide after reports that hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance

By Stephen Culp and Purvi Agarwal

US stocks tumbled on Friday, with the Nasdaq suffering its largest one-day percentage drop since June 5 following disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon, which amplified growing worries surrounding AI-related companies' massive spending on the nascent technology.

All three major US stock indexes slumped, with the Nasdaq sliding 2.9%. The tech-heavy index has dropped 7.8% from its all-time closing high reached on October 6.

The tech rout was sparked by disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon released late on Thursday. While Amazon pared losses as the session progressed, Intel shares plunged 28.6%.

Chip stocks veered sharply lower, with Nvidia down 4.2% and AMD sliding 10.9%. The broader chips index shed 7.2%, slumping to a monthly loss of more than 15%. Server makers Dell and HP dropped 10.8% and 9.6%, respectively.

"It's fair to say that this week, not just today, has been very much about the future of AI and what that's going to look like, whether there will be a positive return on investment and if so, how quickly," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president at Wealthspire Advisors in New York.

"Companies that are performing and meeting the very lofty expectations that have been set are doing well," Pursche added. "Those that are falling short and seem to be missing the mark or not executing as expected are getting punished."

All three main equity indexes closed lower on the week. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq logged monthly losses, while the Dow exited October with a gain.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX lost 140.32 points, or 1.82%, to 7,580.07 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 747.73 points, or 2.86%, to 25,437.00.

The S&P 500 tech sector posted its largest monthly percentage loss since March 2025, and communication services registered its biggest monthly drop since April 2022.

Third-quarter earnings season has passed the halfway mark, with 299 companies in the S&P 500 having reported. Of those, 82% have beaten consensus expectations, according to LSEG data.

Analysts now expect third-quarter S&P 500 earnings growth of 31.6%, year-on-year, per LSEG.

Oil supermajors Exxon Mobil and Chevron both beat quarterly profit expectations, benefiting from soaring profit margins as a result of energy supply disruptions arising from the US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine. The stocks gained 2.2% and 2.8%, respectively.

Starbucks dipped 1.8% after the coffee chain forecast an annual revenue decline due to its divestiture of its Chinese business.

Cryptocurrency-related firms Coinbase , Strategy , and Robinhood fell between 7.2% and 10.6% in the wake of reports that hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.8-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 169 new highs and 377 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 1,196 stocks rose and 3,622 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.03-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 43 new 52-week highs and 5 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 70 new highs and 355 new lows.

Volume on US exchanges was 19.87 billion shares, compared with the 17.26 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

data.title: Treasury Yields End Month With Large Declines — Market Talk
data.description:
1619 ET - Treasury yields end October sharply lower as a flight to safety turns September's historic selloff into a bond-buying spree. Binance's $6.3 billion heist spooks equity investors already wary about massive investment in AI. Attention now turns to midterms on Tuesday and the Treasury quarterly refunding plans to be announced Wednesday. Investors will watch for indications of how quickly the Treasury plans to reduce long-term debt issuance in favor of short-term bills. The 10-year yield falls 0.364 percentage point in October, to 4.928%, its largest monthly decline since December 2023. The two-year sheds 0.306 point to 4.579%, its largest one-month drop since August 2025. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1543 ET - Earnings per share growth from five of the "Magnificent 7" companies has so far lagged other names in the S&P 500 Index in the third quarter, per FactSet earnings analyst John Butters. Nvidia and Apple have yet to report their most recent earnings, but the estimated blended earnings growth rate for the group of megacap tech stocks has fallen to 22.6% from 33.6% a month ago, Butters says. That compares with a 32.6% blended growth rate for the other 493 companies in the index, meaning Mag 7 earnings growth is on track to fall below the rest of the index for the first time since the fourth quarter of 2022. Surveyed analysts expect the trend to hold in the fourth quarter this year.(elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1419 ET - Days after raising its policy rate by a quarter point, the Bank of Canada faces a reality check over its outlook for accelerating growth, says David Rosenberg, head of market-strategy firm Rosenberg Research. Data covering non-farm payrolls indicate a 49,600 decline in jobs in August. Further, GDP stalled in August, and is expected to contract in September--leading to annualized growth of 1.3% in 3Q, or well below the BOC's 2% forecast. "Can the central bank really ignore the economy and this recent squishy-soft set of economic data?," says Rosenberg about pending rate hikes. He argues BOC based its rate-hike decision on "dubious surveys instead of facts on the ground," adding there is no evidence of elevated fuel prices spilling over to non-energy goods. (paul.vieira@wsj.com, @paulvieira)

1306 ET - GDP data for Canada indicates that the solid growth envisaged by the Bank of Canada into 2027 "remains very tenuous," says Carl Gomez, chief economist at Toronto-based Centurion Asset Management. Via a post on LinkedIn, Gomez says GDP in Canada may struggle to grow over 1% annualized in 3Q, whereas BOC forecast 2%. "The takeaway," Gomez says, "is that the BOC's rate-hiking cycle is unlikely to be a protracted one," and will have to monitor incoming data to before tightening financial conditions further. He anticipates one more BOC rate hike in early 2027, although he says he doesn't expect policymakers "going much further unless the actual data warrants it."(paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1257 ET - It's a tough day for tech stocks, but tech bull Yorkville Ives cautions against panicking. The analysts say in a note that results from hyperscalers over the past two weeks further validate the case for the enterprise AI buildout. "This requires patience and it's easy to sell the tech winners during these times of turmoil," they say. Still, "valuations across the tech franchise are not expensive with growth prospects that are likely stunning into the next few years," Yorkville Ives says. The firm expects AI returns to more clearly justify capital spending next year, at which point investors will "see the light." Tech stocks are selling off broadly, headlined by a 30% plunge in Intel.(elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1248 ET - The breaches at Binance and Polymarket will make recovery spending a budget priority, presenting a potential boon for Rubrik's identity and data recovery products, Wedbush analyst Steven Wahrhaftig says in a research note. The increasing frequency of attacks widens the set of buyers for whom recovery is a necessity rather than an option, and rising incident costs are boosting the value of platforms that can provide clients with a clean restore, the analyst says. He expects Rubrik's annualized recurring revenue from net new subscriptions, and its count of customers spending $100,000 or more, will accelerate over the next two quarters as more breach-driven recovery budgets are approved. Rubrik shares are down 10% at $119.28. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1247 ET - Church & Dwight's stronger gross margins helped offset higher global transportation rates and inflationary pressures. Gross margins expanded 170 basis points to 46.8% in 3Q thanks to higher volume, manufacturing productivity, tariff refunds and a favorable mix from acquisitions. "While there are growing inflationary pressures related to the Middle East conflict and transportation rates are increasing globally, the Company is confident it can continue to mitigate this cost pressure," CEO Rick Dierker says. The company now sees full-year adjusted gross margin expanding by approximately 100 basis points, inclusive of those incrementally higher transportation costs.(adriano.marchese@wsj.com)

1230 ET - Investors are selling off tech stocks amid mounting fears of AI. But the selloff hasn't resulted in a buy-in to consumer stocks, where strong underlying data and impressive prints haven't been rewarded like they should, Mizuho analysts say in a research note. "We believe consumer is still under-owned here," they write, pointing to a solid underlying fundamentals and a strong earnings season so far within the group. The analysts speculate there may be some hesitation around the upcoming holiday season and next week's midterm elections. "We advise clients to keep their guard up and stay selective over the next few months," they write, selecting Walmart, Costco and O'Reily as their highest-quality picks. (connor.hart@wsj.com)

1227 ET - Intel's commentary around server supply growth doesn't provide a fully satisfying answer as to why the company continues to forecast meaningful relief in the second half of 2027, StoneX analyst Cody Acree writes in a note. "If server demand has been visible and expanding, and increasing server supply has been a management priority, the fact that the larger revenue step still waits until 2H27 suggests the constraint cannot be explained by a single late-arriving component," Acree writes. "The relevant question is not whether wafer, substrate and assembly lead times are real - they are - but why the combined system was not positioned earlier to respond to demand that management describes as unusually strong." There's more execution risk around capacity that Intel's confidence suggests, he adds. Shares fall 30% to $64.69. (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1204 ET - The long-term investment thesis for crypto isn't changed by the $6.3 billion Binance hack, but the bar is raised for platforms that want to ride the next wave of growth, Moon Pursuit Capital's Utkarsh Ahuja says in a note. Investors will start to favor platforms that demonstrate robust security, transparency and independently verifiable safeguards, rather than just liquidity and execution, he says. "Trust can no longer be assumed; it has to be earned," Ahuja says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1203 ET - Morgan Stanley analysts don't find the Intel investment case compelling, even after PC softness in the third quarter triggers a 29% drop in the stock price. Beyond the third-quarter weakness, Intel failed to deliver what the analysts say would build more confidence in the stock: a path to leadership in the CPU market. "Intel describes 2027 as an investment year, but even with the high capital spending requirements, it is clear to us that it will lose share to fabless competitors that have no such requirement, with AMD, NVIDIA, Graviton and Axion all materially outgrowing Intel's 30% market growth rate in CPU next year," the analysts write. Intel's multiple should be dampened if the CPU shortage is temporary, they add. (elias.schisgall@wsj.com)

1201 ET - The $6.3 billion Binance hack is a reminder that the biggest vulnerability in crypto is the infrastructure and operational controls around the blockchain, not the blockchain itself, Moon Pursuit Capital's Utkarsh Ahuja says in a note. For institutional investors, it highlights the need for independent custody, segregated assets, multi-layered transaction authorization and limiting exposure to a single exchange, he says. For retail investors, this should advance the conversation around safer custody solutions for everyone, Ahuja says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

(e) On October 27, 2026, the Compensation Committee (the "Committee") of PBF Energy Inc.'s (the "Company") Board of Directors approved grants of long-term incentive awards effective as October 27, 2026 (the "Grant Date") under the Company's 2025 Equity Incentive Plan (as amended, the "Equity Incentive Plan") as follows: Matthew C. Lucey, the Company's Chief Executive Officer & President received a 2026 long-term incentive award of $8,484,700 and each of Joseph Marino, Senior Vice President & Chief Financial Officer, T. Paul Davis, Senior Vice President, Supply, Trading and Optimization, and Trecia Canty, Senior Vice President, General Counsel & Secretary, received a 2026 long-term incentive award of $2,500,000. The foregoing 2026 long-term incentive awards were allocated (i) 40% to restricted shares of the Company's Class A common stock ("Common Stock"), (ii) 30% to performance share units for the three-year performance period from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2029 (the "Performance Period"), payable in shares of Common Stock, the amount of which will range from zero to 200 percent of the number of performance share units granted based on TSR performance during the Performance Period as determined by the Committee plus additional shares of Common Stock may be awarded at vesting with respect to the computed value of dividend equivalents accrued during the Performance Period and (iii) 30% to performance units with a target value of $1.00 per unit payable in cash, the amount of which will range from zero to 200 percent of the number of performance units granted based on TSR performance during the Performance Period as determined by the Committee. The restricted stock vests in equal installments over three (3) years and the performance share units and the performance units will vest on December 31, 2029, in each case subject to forfeiture or acceleration under certain circumstances set forth in the applicable award agreement, the forms of which agreements are attached as Exhibits 10.1 and 10.2 to this Form 8-K.

data.title: Canada Deems Vancouver Port Expansion a National Priority in Bid to Diversify Trade — Update
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Canada declared as a national priority a proposed expansion at the country's busiest port in Vancouver, British Columbia, arguing that it is required for the country to meet its goal of doubling non-U.S. exports by 2035.

The designation also kicks off an accelerated regulatory review process, whereby officials are tasked with determining how the expansion proceeds and under what conditions, as opposed to whether it requires approval.

Officials said this puts the timing for a final investment decision from the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority by mid-2027.

"We cannot afford to let bottlenecks hold back Canadian trade," Canadian Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said Friday at a press conference in suburban Vancouver. "The sooner we build the [trade] capacity Canada needs, the sooner Canadian businesses and workers can benefit."

The authority, which manages the Vancouver port, said the expansion project would increase container capacity by about 50%, through a new land-mass and wharf structure covering 300 acres. This additional capacity could support annual trade of 100 billion Canadian dollars (US$71.5 billion).

Officials peg the project's cost at C$5.9 billion. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has pledged up to C$10 billion in financial support for Pacific coast trade corridors.

The port authority said the Vancouver terminal currently handles more than C$1 billion in commerce daily, and more cargo than the next five largest Canadian ports combined.

The expansion, upgrade and construction of trade corridors across Canada is a priority initiative for Carney, who has argued that it is necessary to restore resilience in the economy and reduce the country's reliance on U.S. trade to drive economic growth.

According to government documents, there needs to be a "significant expansion" of Canada's port capacity to diversify trade, adding that 80% of trade with non-U.S. markets is done by sea. The prime minister has set a goal of doubling the level of non-U.S. exports by 2035.

"Continued inaction on port expansion could eventually force Canadian importers and exporters to utilize U.S. ports--a dependency that is untenable in the current geopolitical circumstances," officials said, according to documents distributed at a technical briefing. "Port expansion is thus integral to ensuring Canadian sovereignty and control over key economic linkages to the rest of the world," the officials said, according to the documents.

Officials warned that without port expansion, Canada could face sharply higher shipping costs of up to C$900 million a year due to traffic congestion and insufficient capacity.

Bank of Canada researchers warned this year that the country lacked the port capacity to executive the government's trade agenda.

The central bank's analysis indicated Canadian ports can't accommodate some of the latest ultra-large container ships being deployed. Because of this, some goods originating from China and destined for Canada and loaded onto these big vessels have to dock in Los Angeles--and those goods could be subject to U.S. tariffs.

Write to Paul Vieira at paul.vieira@wsj.com
